For memories with an address type of , this must be a value. "i64" BigInt Return value The previous size of the memory, in units of WebAssembly pages. For memories with an address type of , this must be a value. "i64" BigInt Return value The previous size of the memory, in units of WebAssembly pages. For memories with an address type of , this is a value. "i64" BigInt Exceptions : If the current size added with exceeds the Memory instance's maximum size capacity.

RangeError delta Examples Using grow The following example creates a new WebAssembly Memory instance with an initial size of 1 page (64KiB), and a maximum size of 10 pages (640KiB). js const memory = new WebAssembly.Memory({ initial: 1, maximum: 10, }); We can then grow the instance by one page like so: js const bytesPerPage = 64 * 1024; console.log(memory.buffer.byteLength / bytesPerPage); // "1" console.log(memory.grow(1)); // "1" console.log(memory.buffer.byteLength / bytesPerPage); // "2" Note the return value of here is the previous number of WebAssembly pages. grow() Growing a 64-bit memory For memories with an address type of , pass a value to : "i64" BigInt grow() js const memory = new WebAssembly.Memory({ address: "i64", initial: 1n, maximum: 10n, }); console.log(memory.grow(1n)); // 1n Detachment upon growing Every call to will detach any references to the old , even for ! Detachment means that the 's becomes zero, and it no longer has bytes accessible to JavaScript.

Accessing the property after calling , will yield an with the correct length. grow buffer grow(0) ArrayBuffer byteLength buffer grow ArrayBuffer js const memory = new WebAssembly.Memory({ initial: 1, }); const oldMemoryView = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer); memory.grow(1); // the array is empty! console.log(oldMemoryView); // Uint8Array [] js const memory = new WebAssembly.Memory({ initial: 1, }); memory.grow(1); const currentMemoryView = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer); // the array is full of zeros console.log(currentMemoryView); // Uint8Array(131072) [ 0, 0, 0, ... ] // 131072 = 64KiB * 2 For a shared instance, the initial (which would be a in such case) will not become detached, but rather its length will not be updated. Accesses to the property after growing will yield a larger which may access a larger span of memory than the buffer from before growing the . Every from the property will all refer to the start of the same memory address range, and thus manipulate the same data.

title: grow: Wasm memory instruction - WebAssembly | MDN
excerpt: Try it (module (import "console" "log" (func $log (param i32))) (memory 1 2) ;; start with one memory page, and max of 2 pages (func $main ;; grow memory by 1 page ;; grow returns 1 for success and -1 for failure ;; will fail if you grow to more than 2 pages (memory.grow (i32.const 1)) call $log ;; log the result ) (start $main) ) const url = "{%wasm-url%}"; await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(fetch(url), { console }); Syntax Grow the default (0-index) memory wat ;; Grow default memory by a number of pages indicated by the top value on the stack i32.const 3 ;; Number of pages to grow the memory (3) memory.grow ;; Grow the memory (by 3 pages) ;; the top item on the stack will now either be the previous number of pages (success) or `-1` (failure) ;; grow default memory by two pages using an S-expression (memory.grow (i32.const 2)) Grow a specified memory wat ;; Grow memory with index 1 i32.const 1 ;; Number of pages to grow specified memory (1) memory.grow (memory 1) ;; Grow memory index 1 ;; Grow memory with name $memory1 i32.const 1 ;; Number of pages to grow specified memory (1)

That's shown in the following example. grow For completeness, we can use the compiled version of the above file with code similar to that shown below (the log function is imported into the module, and called by the module): grow.wasm js start(); async function start() { const importObject = { console: { log(arg) { console.log(arg); }, }, }; const result = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming( fetch("grow.wasm"), importObject, ); } start(); Growing a specified memory As memories are defined in a Wasm module they are sequentially allocated an index number from zero. You can grow a specific memory by specifying the instruction and the desired index or name (if it has one), after the instruction.
